Would the Word from God the Father reasonably decline His own things? If the Word is considered in Himself, He is in need of no good, and the Holy Spirit is said to be His own; since, as I said, He became flesh with His own Spirit, anointing His own temple; for the Father works all things through the Son alone in Israel; the Spirit is said to be received economically as a man; for it is said that Jesus from Nazareth was anointed by God with the Holy Spirit and power; but as God, He gives the Spirit to those worthy to receive it; and indeed, He breathed on the holy apostles, saying 'Receive the Holy Spirit', and the divine Peter proclaimed to the Jewish crowds concerning the Spirit, saying that Jesus, having been exalted to the right hand of God, received the promise of the Spirit from the Father and poured it out; you hear in these words that He was exalted to the right hand of God, received and gave the Spirit; He was exalted, of course, when He humbled Himself; just as He willingly humbled Himself for this purpose, so again He exalts Himself, being the hand of the Father by which all things are worked in a godly manner; thus, He is exalted through Himself according to the will of the Father, when, having broken the bonds of death and said to the spirits below 'Come out', He sat at the right hand of the Father; the Son according to nature was anointed with the oil of gladness, when the Father also declared Him to be God, having become so for our sake; but it is not at all absurd to say this;

For he said to the holy apostles 'I am going to my Father and your Father and my God and your God', behold he clearly called his own Father God because of his human nature. Since we have been called to adoption through him, he has given us his Father. But just as we, even if we are called sons of the Father, are human, and we have not ignored the grace of the one who honored us. Thus the natural Son and Lord, even if he recognized God his Father through the flesh and his likeness to us, did not cease to be what he is. How then is it said that he was anointed apart from those who share in him? Let us say as is possible. For we have been anointed with the Holy Spirit, and by nature we have been defined as being such, to the extent that the nature of divinity of all created things is understood. But the Word of God, who became human through us, anoints his own temple with his own Spirit, not imparting a partial energy, nor in a hierarchical order as he gives to us, but rather filling with sanctification and his own power and glory.
pass_b_english: The Word from God the Father would not reasonably decline His own things, for if considered in Himself, He is in need of no good, and the Holy Spirit is said to be His own. Since, as I said, He became flesh with His own Spirit, anointing His own temple, the Father works all things through the Son alone in Israel. The Spirit is said to be received economically, as a man, for it is said that Jesus from Nazareth was anointed by God with the Holy Spirit and power (Luke 4:18).

But as God, He gives the Spirit to those worthy to receive it, and indeed, He breathed on the holy apostles, saying 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:22). The divine Peter proclaimed to the Jewish crowds concerning the Spirit, saying that Jesus, having been exalted to the right hand of God, received the promise of the Spirit from the Father and poured it out (Acts 2:33). You hear in these words that He was exalted to the right hand of God, received and gave the Spirit; He was exalted, of course, when He humbled Himself. Just as He willingly humbled Himself for this purpose, so again He exalts Himself, being the hand of the Father by which all things are worked in a godly manner. He is exalted through Himself according to the will of the Father, when, having broken the bonds of death and having said to the spirits below 'Come out' (Luke 23:43), He sat at the right hand of the Father.

When Jesus said to his apostles, 'I am going to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God' (John 20:17), he clearly referred to his own Father as God, speaking from his human perspective. Through him, we have been called to adoption, and he has given us his Father as our own. Just as we, though called sons of the Father, are still human and have not forgotten the grace of the one who honored us, so too the natural Son and Lord, though he recognized God as his Father through his flesh and his likeness to us, did not cease to be what he is.

The Word of God, who became human through us, anoints his own temple with his own Spirit, not imparting a partial energy, nor in a hierarchical order as he gives to us, but rather filling it with sanctification and his own power and glory. For he said, 'I sanctify myself for their sake, so that they also may be' (John 17:19). We, on the other hand, have been anointed with the Holy Spirit, and by nature, we have been defined as being such, to the extent that the nature of divinity of all created things is understood. How then can it be said that he was anointed apart from those who share in him? Let us consider this question and try to provide an answer.
